accuracy.evidence: Matches the Key Stage 1 science statements in the English national curriculum (Year 2: living things live in habitats to which they are suited), with camouflage as the first example of what Year 6 calls adaptation. Each fact was checked: mountain hares turn white in winter and brown in summer, peppered-moth style bark moths survive best when they match the bark, a tiger's stripes break up its outline in grass, and ladybirds stand out on purpose as a warning.

misconceptions.evidence: Takes on 'white always hides' (the hare must be moved from brown earth to snow, and the prediction trap 'Yes, white always hides'), 'small animals or still animals are hidden' (practice p1 and the 'if it is big' trap), and 'only prey hide' (the tiger step and mastery m3). The adult notes name each one as a common mistake and add the warning-colour exception.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagcamo is a set of painted habitat scenes: leaves with three caterpillars to tap, bark with a moth you recolour, a split snow and earth scene with a draggable hare, long grass with three tiger coats, and a bird hunt that removes the moths that do not match. It passes the 30% shingle gate and is unlike the habitat sorter and food-chain labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The steps build the idea in order: spot which animal is hardest to see, make an animal match its background, see that the same colour fails on the wrong background, learn that pattern hides outline as well as colour, then watch a predator remove the animals that stand out so only the camouflaged ones are left. The Challenge asks the same ideas with new animals.

predictions.evidence: Five steps ask for a prediction before acting (which caterpillar is found last, is the hare hidden on earth, which tiger is hardest to see, which moths are left). The answer is locked in, and the result quotes it back, for example 'You predicted the striped one: spot on!', or explains why the guess was wrong.

challenge_feedback.evidence: There are six Challenge questions, and every wrong answer gets its own why() reply instead of 'try again'. For example, 'it is very small' for the frog gets 'Size is not the clue. Look at the colour and pattern next to the background.', and 'white always hides' gets 'Camouflage depends on the background. White hides on snow but stands out on brown mud.' Right answers count a streak. A rule card stays above the questions.

readability.evidence: The kid paragraphs are at about Flesch-Kincaid grade 1.7, using short sentences and the words camouflage, blend in, stand out, predator and prey. The adult notes are at grade 6.8. Each lab step has two or three short sentences, and tasks start with a pointing hand and a verb (Tap, Drag, Press Bird hunts).

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph adds a point: the definition, an example of matching, the right-background rule and hunters hiding. The adult notes cover the curriculum link, prey and predator examples, seasonal coats, disruptive colouring, named mistakes, a walk-through of the lab and a hide-and-seek home activity. There is no padding, and the content gate's similarity is under 12%.

mobile.evidence: Checked at phone width on iPhone in dark and Android in light. The scenes fill the width, animals are big tap targets with generous hit areas, and the hare drag also has Move to snow and Move to earth buttons. Option buttons wrap at least 44 px tall, and nothing scrolls sideways.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas has an aria-label and a live caption that says what is in each scene in words ('Eight moths rest on brown bark: three brown, one yellow...'). Every tap or drag has a button version. Colour names are written on the buttons, so the colour itself is not the only cue. Contrast passes in light and dark, and sound is off by default.

sources: Department for Education (2013) National curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Year 2 Living things and their habitats; Year 6 Evolution and inheritance (adaptation)
